decision.quote:
In sum,

children tended to associate multiplication and division with fraction–natural number

combinations and addition and subtraction with two fractions, regardless of denominators.

Occasionally, unequal-denominator fractions were also linked to multiplication or division.

While children’s responses largely reflected textbook patterns, these unexpected

observations point to fruitful directions for future research. Overall, these results complement

the findings of Braithwaite and Siegler (2018), suggesting that children learn spurious

association from their textbook fraction arithmetic problem distributions.
decision.rationale: Babari et al. (2025) replicate Braithwaite & Siegler (2018) across Study 1 (textbook analysis) and Study 2 (6th-grade Fraction-Test). First, Study 1 explicitly replicates the original overarching phenomenon: 'Replicating prior research, the results of Study 1 revealed nonrandom and unbalanced distributions between arithmetic operations and operand features in both decimal and fraction problems' (Abstract, p. 2; Discussion, p. 35). Second, the difference between Swiss and U.S. textbooks (Swiss textbooks contain almost no equal-denominator fraction problems, at 3%-5%, and instead pair addition/subtraction with unequal denominators) is not a failed replication of an effect; rather, it provides the natural curricular variation that Study 2 uses to test Braithwaite & Siegler's core associative-learning hypothesis ('Given that the distributions of problems in Swiss mathematics textbooks differ for some combinations of operation and operands from the ones in U.S. textbooks, our pattern of expected associations diverges slightly from the one found by Braithwaite and Siegler (2018)', p. 18). Third, across the original tasks (Tasks 1, 3, and 4) in Study 2, children's operation-operand associations mirrored their Swiss textbooks, and the authors explicitly conclude in the Abstract ('The results of Study 2 revealed that sixth graders' associations mirrored those found in textbooks, suggesting that children learn spurious associations from the distribution of arithmetic problems in textbooks', p. 2) and Discussion ('Overall, these results complement the findings of Braithwaite and Siegler (2018), suggesting that children learn spurious association from their textbook fraction arithmetic problem distributions', p. 36; see also 'consistent with the findings of Braithwaite and Siegler (2018)', p. 38) that the replication succeeded. The two 'X' marks in Table 3 do not constitute failures of tested original findings: Task 5 is a novel added task not in Braithwaite & Siegler (2018) whose responses were confounded by a first-option order bias (pp. 36-37), and the equal-denominator cell in Task 1 reflects the near-absence (3%-5%) of equal-denominator problems in Swiss textbooks (where the authors' actual Swiss-textbook prediction in text was for unequal denominators, which was strongly supported in Tasks 1 and 2 with PD = 99.99% and 100%, 0.01% in ROPE). The remaining dagger marks in Tasks 3 and 4 represent effects in the predicted direction (PD = 91.47%-99.15%) that overlapped the Bayesian small-effect ROPE. Under the codebook, both the authors' explicit overall verdict and the original-specific empirical comparisons establish outcome = 'successful'.

decision.quote: The original result is thus replicated, consistent with that a declining fundamental value increases mispricing (i.e prices different than the F V ). The relative effect size of the replication is 30.42% (0.108/0.355). These results are also shown in the table below. In the original study the relative deviation (RD), which is a measure of the direction of the mispricing, expressing either overpricing or underpricing, is also compared between treatments t1 and t2. For completeness we report the results for RD in the original study and the replication in the table below as well. In the original study RD is 0.297 in treatment t1 and −0.060 in treatment t2 and this difference (the effect size) of 0.357 is significant (p < 0.01 with a Mann-Whitney test). In the replication the RD is 0.031 in treatment t1 and 0.044 in treatment t2, and the difference in RD is −0.013. This difference is not significant using the same test as in the original study (p = 0.375). We thus cannot confirm that a declining fundamental value increases overpricing. The difference in the studies here is that we do not observe any significant overpricing in treatment t1 in the replication.
decision.rationale: In the individual replication report for Kirchler, Huber, & Stöckl (2012) ('Replication of "Thar She Blows: Can Bubbles Be Rekindled with Experienced Subjects?"', line 1337), the Analysis section explicitly defines the replication scope as: 'The research question of interest for this replication is "RQ2: Does a declining fundamental value lead to mispricing and/or overvaluation?"' from Table 6 (p. 875) of the original paper. Table 1 of the replication report compares treatments t1 and t2 on both original measures from that research question: relative absolute deviation (RAD, measuring mispricing) and relative deviation (RD, measuring overpricing/overvaluation). While the treatment difference in RAD was statistically significant in the same direction as the original study (0.157 vs. 0.049, difference = 0.108, Mann-Whitney p = 0.010, relative effect size 30.42%), the treatment difference in RD failed to replicate (0.031 vs. 0.044, difference = -0.013, Mann-Whitney p = 0.375, vs. original difference 0.357, p < 0.01), and the authors explicitly contrast this failure: 'We thus cannot confirm that a declining fundamental value increases overpricing. The difference in the studies here is that we do not observe any significant overpricing in treatment t1 in the replication.' The boilerplate Discussion sentence ('Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α = 5%') refers specifically to the primary RAD criterion used for EERP summary scoring and does not resolve the replication of Kirchler et al. (2012) as a whole into a unitary success across both tested original outcomes. Under Codebook Step 3 Rules 1 and 2, because RAD succeeded while RD failed to replicate within the same tested comparison, the outcome for this target paper is 'mixed'.

Although the individual OSF replication report for Kessler & Roth (2012, AER; Ref. 47) timed out during source acquisition and is absent from the merged text file, Camerer et al. (2016) explicitly document both the single tested original hypothesis and its replication outcome in the main text and supplementary materials. As explained in the main text ('For simplicity, we focused on the dozen studies having one central treatment effect between subjects, and in the remaining six studies, we selected the most central treatment comparison (table S2)', lines 108-110; see also Supplement Section 1, lines 601-610, Section 2, lines 669-671, and Table S2, lines 1179-1182), the EERP team selected one specific between-subjects treatment comparison for Kessler & Roth (2012) and experimentally ran only the two treatments required for that test ('Probability of registering as an organ donor was significantly higher under an "opt-in+" frame than under a neutral "opt-in" frame in rounds 1-15 of the game'). Table S1 (line 1269) reports that the original effect (r = 0.49, p < 0.001, N* = 288) was statistically significant in the same direction in the replication (r = 0.34, p = 0.016, N* = 48, relative effect size 0.71) and explicitly classifies the study as 'Replicated: Yes' (and Figure 1 / lines 155-159 include Kessler & Roth 2012 among the 11 successfully replicated studies). Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1, this explicit author classification settles outcome = 'successful'.

decision.rationale: Although the individual OSF replication report for Duffy & Puzzello (2014, AER; Ref. 39) timed out during source acquisition and is absent from the merged text file, Camerer et al. (2016) explicitly document both the tested original hypothesis and its replication outcome in the main text and supplementary materials. Per the main text (lines 108-110), Supplement Sections 1-2 (lines 601-610, 669-671), and Table S2 (lines 1163-1165), the EERP replication tested the central between-subjects comparison from Duffy & Puzzello (2014) ('Average efficiency (measured cleanly by consumption rate of a non-production good, normalized by the first-best consumption rate) was significantly higher in monetary than in non-monetary economies in the first parts of each of the two sessions'), running only the two treatments required for that test. Table S1 (line 1261) reports that whereas the original study found r = 0.76, p = 0.010 (N* = 54), the replication found a non-significant effect in the opposite direction, r = −0.12, p = 0.674 (N* = 96, relative effect size −0.15), and explicitly classifies the study as 'Replicated: No' (see also main text lines 155-170 and Figure 1). Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1, this explicit author classification settles outcome = 'failed'.
